items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports an indirect-effect claim (predator limits a prey's foraging range and so its effect on a forest); key needs a wolf-free comparison and the forest outcome
items.passage: Beavers are central place foragers: they leave the safety of their ponds to cut trees and shrubs on land, then haul the branches back to the water along established feeding trails. Tracking wolves and beavers in northern Minnesota, Thomas Gable and colleagues found that wolves ambush beavers beside these trails and kill them on longer trails more often than would be expected from how frequently beavers use such trails. Because beavers’ cutting reshapes the forest surrounding wetlands, the researchers argue that wolves, by constraining how far from water beavers forage, indirectly limit the extent of forest that beavers transform.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ argument?
options: In years when beavers in the study area were abundant, wolves killed more beavers, on average, than in years when beavers were scarce, regardless of how long the beavers’ feeding trails were.
Beavers in the study area made more trips per night along long feeding trails than along short ones, and they also spent more time on land during each of those trips.
Around wetlands where wolves had long been absent, beavers’ feeding trails reached farther inland, and the strip of forest beavers cut was wider, than around similar wetlands with wolves.
Beavers whose feeding trails were often visited by wolves kept using those trails in later years, cutting trees at about the same distances from the water as before.
items.explanation: The researchers argue that wolves, “by constraining how far from water beavers forage, indirectly limit the extent of forest that beavers transform.” To support this, a finding has to show that where wolves are missing, beavers forage farther from water and change more of the forest. Choice C does both: without wolves, feeding trails reach farther inland and the strip of forest cut by beavers is wider than around similar wetlands with wolves.

A.recipe: OFF: right animals, different variable (how many beavers are killed)
A.why_wrong: This links wolf kills to how many beavers there are, not to how far beavers forage, and it says nothing about how much forest beavers alter.

B.recipe: PART: explains why long trails are risky but stops before foraging distance and forest
B.why_wrong: More trips and more time on land would explain why beavers on long trails are easy targets, but the finding does not show that wolves keep beavers closer to water or that this changes how much forest beavers cut.

D.recipe: OPP: beavers do not shorten their foraging range under wolf pressure
D.why_wrong: If beavers kept cutting trees just as far from the water despite wolf visits, wolves would not be limiting how far beavers forage, which weakens the argument.

sources.what: Gable, Johnson-Bice, Homkes, Fieberg, Bump 2023, Proc. R. Soc. B 290: 20231377: wolves wait in ambush and kill beavers on longer feeding trails than expected from beaver availability; beavers are central place foragers; wolves constrain how far from water beavers forage, which limits the area of forest beavers alter; study in the Greater Voyageurs Ecosystem, Minnesota (full text)

items.notes: Band 6: the key needs a wolf-free comparison group and both links of the argument (foraging distance and forest altered). B is accurate to the study (more trips and more time on land on long trails) but stops at vulnerability; A is off-target (kill numbers); D is the opposite. Rounded details: 'drag the wood back ... along well-worn feeding trails' is general description of beaver foraging.

band7.why: Plan cell 6. The key needs a wolf-free comparison group and both links of the argument (foraging distance, forest altered); B is true to the study but stops at vulnerability, D is the opposite, A off-target. One bridge, no missing premise, so a fair band 6.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a no-harm conclusion from a case-control study; the key needs the change on the treated street measured against the change on the comparison street
items.passage: Merchants frequently oppose replacing on-street parking with bike lanes, anticipating that they will lose customers who arrive by car. In 2016, the city of Toronto removed 136 parking spaces from a stretch of Bloor Street, a busy downtown retail corridor, and installed a pilot bike lane. To determine the lane’s effects, Daniel Arancibia and colleagues surveyed merchants and shoppers both on Bloor Street and on a comparable retail street that received no bike lane, before and during the pilot. Based on these surveys, the researchers concluded that the bike lane had no negative economic impact on businesses along Bloor Street.
items.stem: Which finding from Arancibia and colleagues’ surveys, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ conclusion about the bike lane?
options: From before the pilot to during it, average monthly customer spending rose by a larger percentage on Bloor Street than on the comparison street.
During the pilot, customers on Bloor Street spent more money per month, on average, than customers on the comparison street did.
From before the pilot to during it, merchants on the comparison street reported a larger increase in customers served than merchants on Bloor Street did.
During the pilot, shoppers on Bloor Street who arrived by bicycle spent less per visit, on average, but visited more often than shoppers who arrived by car.
items.explanation: The researchers surveyed “a comparable retail street that received no bike lane, before and during the pilot.” Business on any street can rise or fall for reasons that have nothing to do with a bike lane, so the change on that street shows roughly how Bloor Street would have fared without one. To show that the bike lane did no harm, then, Bloor Street’s change from before the pilot to during it must be compared with the comparison street’s change over the same period. If spending rose by a larger percentage on Bloor Street than on the street with no bike lane, Bloor Street did at least as well as it would have without the bike lane, so choice A supports the conclusion.

B.recipe: TRAP: mismatched comparison (levels at one time, not changes)
B.why_wrong: Comparing the two streets only during the pilot ignores where each started; Bloor Street may have had higher spending before the bike lane and still lost ground during the pilot, so this does not show the bike lane did no harm.

C.recipe: OPP: Bloor Street lags the comparison street
C.why_wrong: If the comparison street gained more customers than Bloor Street over the same period, Bloor Street did worse than it would likely have done without the bike lane, which suggests the bike lane may have hurt business.

D.recipe: TRAP: looks like a test but cannot decide the overall effect
D.why_wrong: Knowing that cyclists spend less per visit but visit more often does not say whether total spending on Bloor Street fell, held steady, or rose relative to what would have happened without the bike lane.

sources.what: Arancibia et al. 2019, 'Measuring the Local Economic Impacts of Replacing On-Street Parking With Bike Lanes', Journal of the American Planning Association (article page; blocks scripts, abstract read through the OpenAlex record below)

Arancibia, Farber, Savan, Verlinden, Smith Lea, Allen, Vernich 2019, Journal of the American Planning Association 85(4): 463-481 (abstract): in 2016 Toronto removed 136 on-street parking spots and installed a pilot bike lane on a stretch of Bloor Street, a downtown retail corridor; case-control and pre-post surveys of merchants and shoppers; no negative economic impacts; monthly customer spending and number of customers served both increased on Bloor Street during the pilot

items.notes: Band 7 moves (T1_single): the comparison must discriminate (a difference of differences, as in 09775cbf): the key compares the change on Bloor Street with the change on the comparison street; B is the mismatched-comparison TRAP (levels during the pilot only, as 09775cbf C and D), D is a TRAP that looks like a test but cannot decide, C is the OPP. The fact the key depends on (why a comparison street was surveyed) sits in an earlier sentence. Stem names the study and the conclusion. Source page is the OpenAlex record of the article's abstract (the publisher page blocks scripts; DOI 10.1080/01944363.2019.1638816). The comparison street (Danforth Avenue in the study) is left unnamed. Options are hypothetical findings.

fixes: removed the sentence explaining why a comparison street was surveyed (it handed the student the difference-of-differences logic); the key now needs that unstated premise
explanation and C why_wrong rewritten to match

band7.why: After the fix: the student must supply why a no-lane comparison street matters (an unstated premise) and pick the change-against-change finding; B is a mismatched levels comparison, D looks like a test but cannot decide, C is the opposite. Stem names the study and the conclusion; passage 101 words.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding discriminates two production methods (open-air condensation vs oxygen-restricted distillation); key reaches the method through what the tar lacks
items.passage: Birch tar, an adhesive that early humans used to attach stone points to handles, is the oldest known synthetic substance, and the earliest examples are associated with Neanderthals. Because producing tar was long assumed to require heating birch bark in a sealed, oxygen-deprived environment, Neanderthal tar was widely interpreted as evidence of sophisticated planning. In 2019, however, Patrick Schmidt and colleagues demonstrated that usable tar also accumulates on a stone positioned beside bark burning in open air, a process Neanderthals could easily have discovered accidentally. Later, comparing two pieces of Neanderthal tar from Königsaue, Germany, with tars produced by several Stone Age methods, Schmidt’s team concluded that the Königsaue tar was nonetheless manufactured with an oxygen-restricting technique.
items.stem: Which finding from the comparison, if true, would most directly support Schmidt’s team’s conclusion about the Königsaue tar?
options: Of all the reference tars, the ones scraped from stones beside bark burning in open air were the closest match to the overall chemical makeup of the Königsaue tar.
Both pieces of the Königsaue tar contained the chemical markers that distinguish tar made from birch bark from tars and resins made from other trees, such as pine.
The Königsaue tar had been molded around the base of a stone tool, and traces of the wooden handle it once secured were preserved on its surface.
The Königsaue tar contained almost none of the soot and charred bark particles that were abundant in every reference tar scraped from stones beside open fires.
items.explanation: Two methods are in question: tar that collects “on a stone positioned beside bark burning in open air” and tar made with “an oxygen-restricting technique.” If every tar made the open-air way was full of soot and charred bark but the Königsaue tar had almost none, the Königsaue tar cannot have been scraped from a stone beside an open fire, which leaves the oxygen-restricting technique. Choice D therefore supports the team’s conclusion.

A.recipe: OPP: the rival method’s prediction
A.why_wrong: If the open-air tars matched the Königsaue tar best, the Neanderthals there most likely used the simple open-air method, which weakens the team’s conclusion.

B.recipe: TRAP: consistent with both methods
B.why_wrong: Both methods start from birch bark, so either one would produce tar with birch markers; this shows what the tar was made from, not how it was made.

C.recipe: TRAP: a property of use, the same under either method
C.why_wrong: Traces of a tool and handle show that the tar was used for hafting, which tar made by either method could be; they do not show how much oxygen reached the bark when the tar was made.

sources.what: Schmidt, Koch, Blessing, Karakostis, Harvati, Dresely, Charrié-Duhaut 2023, Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences 15: 84: birch tar is the oldest synthetic substance, earliest examples associated with Neanderthals; traditionally read as a proxy for cognition; recent work found tar can be produced with simple processes; chemical comparison of the two Königsaue pieces with a reference collection made with Stone Age techniques shows Neanderthals did not use the simplest method but distilled tar in an underground environment that restricted oxygen flow

Schmidt, Blessing, Rageot, Iovita, Pfleging, Nickel, Righetti, Tennie 2019, PNAS 116: 17707-17711: tar production had been assumed to require heating bark in anaerobic conditions; when birch bark burns close to an adjacent stone under aerobic conditions, birch tar is deposited and can be scraped off

items.notes: Band 7 moves (T1_compete): two named views (open-air condensation from Schmidt et al. 2019 PNAS, and the oxygen-restricting technique); the key reaches the conclusion by an unstated premise (open-air tars carry soot and charred bark, so their absence rules that method out); one OPP (A), two TRAPs consistent with both methods (B, birch markers; C, hafting traces). The 2019 open-air finding is summarized in the 2023 abstract ('birch tar can also be produced with simple processes'); 2019 paper: Schmidt et al., PNAS 116: 17707-17711 ('when birch bark burns close to a vertical to subvertical hard surface, such as an adjacent stone, birch tar is naturally deposited'). Options are hypothetical findings; soot content is not a reported result.

fixes: added the 2019 PNAS source (PMC6731756) for the named open-air finding the key depends on

band7.why: Discrimination check: the open-air account predicts soot and char like every open-air reference tar, so their absence (D) rules it out and leaves the oxygen-restricting method; B and C fit both methods, A fits the rival. The key reaches the conclusion through a premise the passage does not state.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding discriminates competing explanations of a crater (a pingo that grew in a drained lake and burst, vs a meteorite or deep methane); key reaches the pingo account through the site's history
items.passage: A crater tens of meters wide that opened in the permafrost of Russia’s Yamal Peninsula prompted competing explanations, including a meteorite impact and an explosive release of methane migrating upward from natural gas deposits deep beneath the region. Sergey Buldovicz and colleagues argue instead that the crater formed when a pingo—an ice-cored mound of earth—burst. In their account, the pingo developed after a shallow lake dried out, allowing the unfrozen ground that had lain beneath the lake to freeze; as it froze, carbon dioxide dissolved in its water separated from solution, and pressure accumulated until the pingo exploded.
items.stem: Which finding about the crater, if true, would most directly support Buldovicz and colleagues’ explanation?
options: Air sampled near the bottom of the crater soon after it was found held far more methane than did air sampled above the surrounding tundra at the same time.
Satellite images of the site from the decades before the crater opened show a small body of water shrinking and vanishing, then a low hill rising in its place.
Blocks of frozen ground from the crater were thrown more than one hundred meters beyond its rim at the moment it formed.
The crater’s walls expose layers of frozen sand and silt cut through by large wedges of ice, a pattern that is common in permafrost throughout the surrounding region.
items.explanation: Buldovicz and colleagues say the pingo “developed after a shallow lake dried out, allowing the unfrozen ground that had lain beneath the lake to freeze,” and that the pingo then burst. Images showing a small body of water disappearing from the site and a low hill (a pingo) then rising there would match that history step by step, while neither a meteorite impact nor methane rising from deep deposits depends on a lake having dried out at the site. Choice B therefore supports their explanation.

A.recipe: OPP: fits the rival (deep methane) explanation
A.why_wrong: A large amount of methane at the bottom of the crater would point to methane from deep gas deposits, the explanation Buldovicz and colleagues reject; their account involves carbon dioxide.

C.recipe: TRAP: consistent with every explanation
C.why_wrong: A meteorite impact, a methane blowout, and a bursting pingo would all throw debris far from the crater, so this does not favor one explanation over the others.

D.recipe: OFF: a feature of the surrounding permafrost, not of how the crater formed
D.why_wrong: Ice wedges that are common in permafrost throughout the region would be found in the crater walls however the crater formed, so they do not point to a pingo.

sources.what: Buldovicz et al. 2018, Scientific Reports 8: 13534: the Yamal crater (a couple of tens of meters wide) aroused hypotheses including a meteorite impact or migration of deep gas; the authors explain it as the collapse of a large pingo that formed within a thaw lake when it shoaled and dried out, allowing the talik below it to freeze back; carbon dioxide dissolved in the pore water of the unfrozen core reached gas saturation, and the pingo exploded

items.notes: Band 6 (T1_compete with one bridge): the student must recognize that the shrinking water and the rising hill in B are the drained lake and the growing pingo of the authors' account, which the rivals do not need. The carbon dioxide option was removed so the key does not echo the passage. C is a TRAP consistent with all views; A fits the rival; D is irrelevant. Background (general knowledge): the Yamal Peninsula's deep natural gas deposits are mostly methane. Options are hypothetical findings, not reported results.

fixes: crater width set to "tens of meters" as the source gives it (was "several tens")
explanation no longer claims the rival accounts need no mound (gas-blowout accounts also involve a mound); it rests on the dried lake only

band7.why: Plan cell 6. One bridge: the shrinking water and rising hill must be read as the dried lake and the growing pingo; C fits every explanation, A fits the rival, D is irrelevant.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates an indirect claim (reserve as a strategy grounded in a view of men); all four quotations are Cressida in neighboring states
items.passage: Troilus and Cressida is a circa 1602 play by William Shakespeare. Though in love with the Trojan prince Troilus, Cressida conceals her feelings from him, a reticence that Shakespeare suggests is calculated, originating in her understanding of men: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from Troilus and Cressida most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “I love you now; but till now not so much / But I might master it. In faith, I lie; / My thoughts were like unbridled children, grown / Too headstrong for their mother.”
“Yet hold I off. Women are angels, wooing: / Things won are done; joy’s soul lies in the doing. / That she belov’d knows naught that knows not this: / Men prize the thing ungain’d more than it is.”

“Perchance, my lord, I show more craft than love; / And fell so roundly to a large confession / To angle for your thoughts; but you are wise— / Or else you love not; for to be wise and love / Exceeds man’s might; that dwells with gods above.”
“Ah, poor our sex! this fault in us I find, / The error of our eye directs our mind. / What error leads must err; O, then conclude, / Minds sway’d by eyes are full of turpitude.”
items.explanation: The claim has three parts: Cressida holds back her feelings, she does so on purpose, and her reason is what she believes about men. In choice B she says “Yet hold I off” (she keeps her love back) and gives her reason as a rule about men: once a woman is won the pursuit is over, because “Men prize the thing ungain’d more than it is.” Her reserve is therefore a deliberate choice based on how she thinks men value what they have not yet won.

A.recipe: HALF: about controlling her love, with no strategy or view of men
A.why_wrong: Cressida says she once could “master” her love and then admits that her thoughts were too “headstrong” to control; the lines show a struggle she lost, not a calculated reserve based on how men behave.

C.recipe: TRAP: names a strategy (“craft”), but for her confession, not her reserve
C.why_wrong: Here Cressida wonders whether her “large confession” of love was crafty, a way “To angle for” Troilus’s thoughts. The craft she suspects lies in revealing her love, not in keeping it from him, and her remark that no man can be both wise and in love does not explain why she would hold back.

D.recipe: LURE: a general rule about the sexes, but about women’s fickleness
D.why_wrong: This is a maxim about women (“poor our sex”) whose minds follow their eyes, spoken as Cressida turns from Troilus to another man; it concerns her own inconstancy, not a reserve grounded in her understanding of men.

sources.what: Shakespeare, Troilus and Cressida (Project Gutenberg Complete Works, eBook 100): A from Act 3 scene 2, B from Act 1 scene 2 (Cressida's soliloquy), C from Act 3 scene 2, D from Act 5 scene 2; all spoken by Cressida
date: probably written in 1602

items.notes: Band 7 moves (spec/rw/band7/command_of_evidence.md 5, T2): pre-1929 drama, indirect claim ('suggests is calculated and rooted in'), all four options the same speaker in neighboring states (lost self-control, suspected craft, self-reproach about women). The hardest trap is C, which offers 'craft' and a remark about men but attaches the craft to her confession, the opposite of reserve. Quotations copied from Gutenberg 100 with its curly apostrophes; C is Cressida's full five-line speech. Troilus and Cressida checked absent from every official item and from claims.txt and satbank/rw.

band7.why: Pre-1929 drama, indirect claim with three parts (holds back, on purpose, because of what she believes about men); all four options are Cressida. C offers "craft" and a remark about men but attaches the craft to her confession; A is a lost struggle; D is a maxim about women. All four quotations match Gutenberg 100 exactly.

items.subtype: Data description: a two-part claim read through a passage criterion (girls' rate above boys' signals disadvantage) across years; distractors are accurate readings of the wrong cells
items.passage: Under natural circumstances, boys under the age of five die at somewhat higher rates than girls of the same age, largely because boys are biologically more vulnerable in early childhood. Demographers therefore regard an under-five mortality rate that is higher for girls than for boys as a strong indication that girls are disadvantaged, whether in nutrition, medical care, or other resources. Comparing mortality estimates for four South Asian countries, a demographer concluded that girls in India faced such a disadvantage in both 1990 and 2020, although the gap between girls’ and boys’ rates there narrowed considerably over that period.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the demographer’s conclusion?
options: In India, the under-five mortality rate for girls fell from about 132 deaths per 1,000 live births in 1990 to about 34 in 2020, a decline of roughly three-quarters.
In Pakistan, the under-five mortality rate for boys was about 9 deaths per 1,000 live births higher than the rate for girls in 1990 and about 11 deaths per 1,000 higher in 2020.
In 2020, the under-five mortality rate for girls in India was about 4 deaths per 1,000 live births higher than the rate for girls in Bangladesh and about 6 higher than the rate for girls in Nepal.
In India, the under-five mortality rate for girls was about 10 deaths per 1,000 live births higher than the rate for boys in 1990 but only about 1 death per 1,000 higher in 2020.

table.title: Under-Five Mortality Rates in Four South Asian Countries (deaths per 1,000 live births)

items.explanation: The text says demographers regard a mortality rate “that is higher for girls than for boys as a strong indication that girls are disadvantaged.” The demographer’s conclusion has two parts: India’s girls faced that disadvantage in both 1990 and 2020, and the gap between girls’ and boys’ rates narrowed. The table shows India’s rate for girls above the rate for boys in 1990 (131.9 against 122.3, about 10 higher) and in 2020 (33.5 against 32.5, about 1 higher). Choice D gives both differences: girls’ rate was higher in each year, by a margin that shrank from about 10 to about 1.

A.recipe: PART: accurate, girls only (no comparison with boys)
A.why_wrong: This is accurate, but it never compares girls with boys, so it cannot show the disadvantage the text defines or the narrowing of the gap between the two rates.

B.recipe: IRREL: accurate reading of the wrong country
B.why_wrong: This is accurate for Pakistan, but the demographer’s conclusion is about India, and in Pakistan the rate for boys, not girls, was the higher one (about 9 and 11 deaths per 1,000 higher), the usual pattern.

C.recipe: IRREL: accurate comparison on the wrong axis (girls across countries)
C.why_wrong: This is accurate, but it compares girls in India with girls in Bangladesh and Nepal; the text’s criterion compares girls with boys in the same country, so it does not show a disadvantage for India’s girls or a change over time.

items.subtype: Quotation from an art historian supports a claim made inside the text's rebuttal (Paris-period figurative work shares the abstractions' concerns)
items.passage: In 1953 the painter Beauford Delaney left New York, where he had painted vivid scenes of city streets as well as portraits, and relocated to Paris, where he remained for the rest of his life. His work there shifted dramatically toward abstract studies of color and light, many of them saturated with an intense yellow. This transformation is sometimes treated as a clean break, with the Paris abstractions regarded as an achievement separate from his figurative painting. Such a view, however, overlooks the fact that the figurative works Delaney produced in Paris, such as his 1963 portrait of the writer James Baldwin, pursue the same concerns as his abstractions.
items.stem: Which quotation from an art historian would most directly support the claim made in the text?
options: “The portraits Delaney made of friends after he settled in Paris are often treated as mere likenesses, but in them each face emerges from the same dense yellows and restless strokes that fill his abstract canvases of those years; what absorbs him is how color seems to give off light.”

“Delaney’s move to Paris marks a decisive turn in his career: once he committed himself to abstraction, the crowded street scenes and portraits that had defined his New York years gave way to a body of work that has little in common with anything he had painted before.”

“Even Delaney’s New York street scenes, painted decades before his abstractions, reveal a fascination with how light falls on buildings and pavement, which suggests that the abstract work he produced in Paris grew out of concerns he had developed long before he ever left the United States for France.”

“Delaney’s portrait of Baldwin records a friendship that sustained the painter through years of poverty and illness in Paris; Baldwin, for his part, wrote that Delaney had been menaced by his circumstances more than any man he knew, and had transcended them more fully.”
items.explanation: The text claims that “the figurative works Delaney produced in Paris, such as his 1963 portrait of the writer James Baldwin, pursue the same concerns as his abstractions,” which are “abstract studies of color and light.” Choice A says that in the portraits Delaney made after he settled in Paris, each face emerges from “the same dense yellows and restless strokes that fill his abstract canvases of those years,” and that what absorbs him is “how color seems to give off light.” Portraits are figurative works, so the quotation shows Delaney’s Paris figurative work pursuing the concerns of his abstractions, which supports the claim.

B.recipe: OPP: sides with the view the text rejects
B.why_wrong: This quotation describes the Paris abstractions as having “little in common” with Delaney’s figurative painting, which is the “clean break” view that the text argues against.

C.recipe: TRAP: a continuity argument, but through the New York works
C.why_wrong: This links the abstractions to Delaney’s New York street scenes, not to the figurative works he made in Paris, so it argues a different continuity from the one the text claims.

D.recipe: HALF: names the text’s own example (the Baldwin portrait) but its personal meaning rather than its artistic concerns
D.why_wrong: This discusses the Baldwin portrait, the work the text names, but only as a record of friendship and hardship; it says nothing about color or light, so it does not show that the portrait pursues the same concerns as the abstractions.

The text's 'clean break' framing and the rebuttal are the passage's own argument, attributed to no real person.

items.subtype: Data completion: a result that contradicts the stated expectation (covered flowers can set fruit only from their own pollen; the most domesticated plants set the least)
items.passage: Many domesticated crops are self-compatible: unlike many of their wild relatives, they can produce fruit using their own pollen. Lislie Solís-Montero and colleagues hypothesized that domestication had favored self-compatibility in tomatillo (Physalis philadelphica), a Mexican fruit crop whose commercial varieties, traditional landraces, and weedy wild forms grow close to one another. The team enclosed flowers on plants of all three types to exclude pollinators, so that any fruit could develop only if a flower pollinated itself, and later recorded several reproductive traits. Contrary to the researchers’ hypothesis, they found that ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: commercial plants produced about 169 ovules per flower, on average, roughly three times as many as weedy plants, which produced the fewest ovules of the three types of plants.
seeds from the enclosed flowers of weedy plants germinated at a lower rate, about 22 percent, than seeds from the enclosed flowers of either commercial plants or landraces did.
only about 11 percent of the enclosed flowers on commercial plants set fruit, compared with about 43 percent on landraces and about 72 percent on weedy plants.
the share of enclosed flowers that set fruit increased with the degree of domestication, reaching its highest level, about 72 percent, among the commercial plants.

table.title: Reproductive Traits of Three Types of Tomatillo Plants
columns: Germination of seeds from enclosed flowers (%)

items.explanation: Because pollinators were kept away, an enclosed flower could set fruit “only if a flower pollinated itself,” so the share of enclosed flowers that set fruit shows how well each type of plant produces fruit from its own pollen. The researchers hypothesized that domestication had favored this ability, so they expected the commercial plants to do best. Instead, the table shows that only about 11 percent of enclosed flowers on commercial plants set fruit, against about 43 percent on landraces and about 72 percent on weedy plants. Choice C states this result, which contradicts the hypothesis.

A.recipe: IRREL: accurate, but a trait unrelated to self-compatibility
A.why_wrong: The ovule figures are accurate, but the number of ovules per flower does not show whether a plant can produce fruit from its own pollen, so it does not contradict the hypothesis.

B.recipe: CONTRA: accurate, but it favors the domesticated plants
B.why_wrong: The germination figures are accurate, but lower germination for weedy plants points the same way as the researchers’ expectation, not against it, and germination is not the measure of fruit set from a flower’s own pollen.

D.recipe: WDIR: the relation applied backward (misplaced value)
D.why_wrong: Fruit set decreased with domestication; about 72 percent is the value for weedy plants, while commercial plants set fruit from only about 11 percent of enclosed flowers.

sources.what: Solís-Montero, Aceves-Chong, Vega-Polanco, Vargas-Ponce 2021, Frontiers in Plant Science 12: 658406: many domesticated plants are self-compatible; hypothesis that artificial selection favors self-compatibility in cultivated P. philadelphica; weedy, landrace and commercial populations coexist in close proximity; contrary to expectations, fruit production by autonomous autogamy was higher in weedy plants; Table 3 fruit set under pollinator exclusion: commercial 11%, landraces 43%, weedy 72%; Table 2 mean ovules 169.3, 94.8, 56.5; Table 5 germination after pollinator exclusion 44%, 46%, 22%

items.notes: Band 7 moves (Q1_P5 surprise, after 9452092c / 3.38): the passage gives only the expectation and the design relation (an enclosed flower can set fruit only from its own pollen), so the student must translate the fruit-set column into self-compatibility and see which group contradicts the hypothesis; options are compound clauses of 25 to 30 words. Checked against the table: A true (169/57 = 3.0; weedy fewest) but irrelevant; B true (22 lowest) but in the expected direction; C true; D false (fruit set falls with domestication; 72 is the weedy value). Ovules rounded to whole numbers; group means from the paper's tables.

Figures for the gross tertiary enrollment ratio—enrollment in universities and other postsecondary institutions divided by the number of people in the five-year age group following secondary school—show that women’s ratio surpassed men’s in Tunisia long before it even matched men’s in Morocco. In 2005, for instance, whereas the ratio for Moroccan women (10.5 percent) remained below that for Moroccan men (12.9 percent), the ratio for ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
options: Tunisian women was 34.0 percent, above the 27.0 percent for Tunisian men.
Tunisian women was 10.2 percent, below the 12.7 percent for Tunisian men.
Tunisian women was 41.5 percent, above the 25.4 percent for Tunisian men.

items.subtype: Data description: a trend that matters only through a passage relation (urban share rises only when urban population grows proportionally faster than total population)
items.passage: The share of a country’s population living in urban areas, a standard measure of urbanization, rises only when the urban population grows proportionally faster than the population as a whole; when the two grow at the same rate, the share remains constant. Tajikistan, a largely mountainous country in Central Asia where most people have long lived in rural villages, became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991, and in the following decades its total population increased substantially. Comparing urban and national population figures for those decades, a geographer concluded that Tajikistan’s urbanization reversed during the 1990s and then stalled over the next twenty years.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the geographer’s conclusion?
options: Tajikistan’s urban population and its total population were both larger in 2020 than they had been in any of the earlier years shown in the table.
Tajikistan’s urban population declined slightly from 1990 to 2000, but it then grew by more than half, rising from about 1.7 million in 2000 to about 2.6 million in 2020.
From 1990 to 2000, Tajikistan’s urban population fell slightly as its total population grew, and from 2000 to 2020, the two populations each grew by a little over half.
Tajikistan’s urban population increased during every decade from 1990 to 2020, although in each of those decades it grew more slowly than the country’s total population did.

table.title: Urban and Total Population of Tajikistan, 1990–2020

items.explanation: The text says the urban share “rises only when the urban population grows proportionally faster than the population as a whole” and stays the same “when the two grow at the same rate.” From 1990 to 2000, the urban population fell (1.72 to 1.67 million) while the total grew (5.40 to 6.28 million), so the urban share fell: urbanization reversed. From 2000 to 2020, both grew by a little more than half (about 53 and 55 percent), so the share stayed almost the same: urbanization stalled. Choice C describes both parts.

A.recipe: IRREL: accurate levels, no comparison of growth
A.why_wrong: Both populations did peak in 2020, but reaching a high level says nothing about whether the urban population grew faster or slower than the total, which is what determines the urban share.

B.recipe: PART: the urban series alone (proxy applied to one column)
B.why_wrong: This is accurate, but it never compares the urban population with the total population; growth of more than half after 2000 would mean rising urbanization only if the total population had grown less, which the choice does not say.

D.recipe: INACC: misreads the 1990s
D.why_wrong: The urban population did not grow from 1990 to 2000; it fell from 1.72 to 1.67 million.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a two-part claim (the stage now seems artificial; the people of Cavendish Square seemed real)
items.passage: Trelawny of the “Wells” is an 1898 play by Arthur Wing Pinero. After a brief residence with her fiancé’s family in Cavendish Square, a fashionable district of London, the actress Rose Trelawny returns to the theater. Pinero suggests that Rose now considers the stage artificial and admires the people she encountered in Cavendish Square: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from Trelawny of the “Wells” most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “I will make you a present of the belt, ’Vonia, if you will accept it. I bought it when I came back to the ‘Wells,’ thinking everything would go on as before. But—it’s of no use; they tell me I cannot act effectively any longer.”
“The truth is, it isn’t as nice as you’d think it. I suppose the Profession had its drawbacks—mother used to say so—but one could fly.”
“How badly I behaved in Cavendish Square! how unlike a young lady! What if the old folks were overbearing and tyrannical, Arthur could be gentle with them.”
“[The theater] isn’t the world we live in, merely a world—such a queer little one! I was less than a month in Cavendish Square, and very few people came there; but they were real people—real!”
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Rose now finds the stage artificial, and she admires the people she met in Cavendish Square. In choice D she says the theater “isn’t the world we live in” but only “a queer little one,” and she says the few people she met in Cavendish Square were “real people,” a point she stresses by repeating “real.” Only this quotation shows both her new view of the theater and her admiration for the people of Cavendish Square.

A.recipe: HALF: the theater part only (she can no longer act), with no view of Cavendish Square
A.why_wrong: Rose says she can no longer act well, which shows that something has changed, but she does not call the stage artificial or say anything about the people she met in Cavendish Square.

B.recipe: OPP: spoken during her stay, preferring the stage’s freedom
B.why_wrong: Rose says life with the Gowers “isn’t as nice as you’d think” and that on the stage “one could fly,” which favors the theater over Cavendish Square, the reverse of the claim.

C.recipe: HALF: Cavendish Square only, and the old people called “overbearing and tyrannical”
C.why_wrong: Rose regrets her own behavior and praises Arthur’s gentleness, but she calls the older Gowers “overbearing and tyrannical” and says nothing about the stage being artificial.

sources.what: Pinero, Trelawny of the “Wells” (Project Gutenberg eBook 47561): A, C and D from Act 3 (Rose at Mrs. Mossop’s lodgings after leaving the Gowers), B from Act 2 (in Cavendish Square); all spoken by Rose
1898 comic play by Arthur Wing Pinero about an actress who tries to give up the stage for love

items.notes: CB-style adaptation: Gutenberg's straight apostrophes curled; double hyphens set as closed em dashes; italics markers dropped; bracketed gloss [The theater] (D; source 'It', which refers to the stage world named in the previous sentence); A ends at 'any longer' (source has a trailing dash); B omits the stage direction [raising her arms] between 'but' and 'one could fly'. Gloss 'a wealthy part of London' added to the setup.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a claim about a cue that replaces gravity (light orients spiders in orbit); key needs the lights-on versus lights-off contrast
items.passage: On Earth, golden silk orb-weaver spiders construct asymmetric webs, with the central hub positioned near the top, and they wait for prey on the hub facing downward, behaviors thought to depend on gravity. To investigate, Samuel Zschokke and colleagues sent two juvenile orb-weavers to the International Space Station, where the spiders were photographed every five minutes for two months as the lamps in their enclosure switched on and off. The researchers concluded that in the absence of gravity, the direction of light can serve as an orientation guide for the spiders.
items.stem: Which finding from the experiment, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ conclusion?
options: The spiders on the space station spun webs that contained roughly the same amount of silk as webs spun by spiders of the same species in a matching enclosure on Earth.
While the lamps were on, the spiders on the space station built webs with the hub shifted toward the light and faced away from it, but while the lamps were off, they showed no consistent direction.

The spiders on the space station built new webs less often during their first few weeks in orbit than they did during their final few weeks there, once they had adjusted to their unfamiliar surroundings.
Spiders kept in a matching enclosure on Earth built webs with the hub near the top and faced downward on the hub regardless of whether the lamps in their enclosure were on or off.
items.explanation: The researchers concluded that “in the absence of gravity, the direction of light can serve as an orientation guide for the spiders.” If, without gravity, the spiders’ webs and resting direction lined up with the light when the lamps were on but had no consistent direction when the lamps were off, then light, not something else, was orienting them. Choice B describes that pattern.

A.recipe: OFF: right spiders, different variable (amount of silk)
A.why_wrong: How much silk the webs contained says nothing about which direction the spiders built their webs or faced, so it does not show that light guided their orientation.

C.recipe: OFF: a change over time, not a response to light
C.why_wrong: Building webs more often after an adjustment period shows the spiders adapting to orbit, but it does not link their orientation to the direction of light.

D.recipe: SUBJ: the Earth spiders, which have gravity
D.why_wrong: Spiders on Earth still have gravity to orient by, so their behavior with the lamps on or off does not show what guides spiders when gravity is absent.

sources.what: Zschokke, Countryman, Cushing 2021 (online 2020), The Science of Nature 108: 1: two juvenile Trichonephila clavipes on the ISS and two Earth controls photographed every 5 minutes for 2 months; Trichonephila normally build asymmetric webs with the hub near the upper edge and face downward on the hub; webs built with the lights on were more asymmetric (hub near the lights), spiders faced away from the lights when on and had random orientation when off; conclusion: in the absence of gravity, the direction of light can serve as an orientation guide

items.notes: Medium T1: the key operationalizes the claim with the needed contrast (lights on against lights off, without gravity). D is the wrong-subject trap (Earth controls still have gravity). 'Golden silk orb-weaver' is the common name of Trichonephila clavipes. Key B is the actual reported pattern, stated as a finding.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a causal claim (disturbed nights disrupt a coordinated morning departure); key observes the outcome after the cause varies
items.passage: Jackdaws (Corvus monedula) spend winter nights in large communal roosts, and in the morning the birds typically depart together, a collective movement they coordinate through their calls. Monitoring roosts in areas that differed in their degree of urbanization, Hannah Broad and colleagues found that where background noise was louder, jackdaws took longer to settle in the evening and called more during the night. The researchers suggest that this nocturnal calling, a probable sign of disrupted sleep, interferes with the birds’ ability to coordinate their morning departures.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ suggestion?
options: On mornings after nights with the most calling, the jackdaws left their roost in scattered groups over a longer period rather than departing together.
Jackdaws at roosts in the noisiest areas arrived at their roosts later in the evening, on average, than jackdaws at roosts in quieter, less urbanized areas did.
Roosts in more urbanized areas were occupied by more jackdaws, on average, than roosts in less urbanized areas were.
Jackdaws departed their roosts in a tightly synchronized group just as often after nights of heavy calling as after quiet nights.
items.explanation: The researchers suggest that nighttime calling “interferes with the birds’ ability to coordinate their morning departures.” If the jackdaws left in scattered groups over a longer period on the mornings after the noisiest nights, rather than departing together, then heavy calling at night would be linked to poorer coordination in the morning. Choice A describes that pattern.

B.recipe: OFF: evening arrival, not morning coordination
B.why_wrong: Arriving later in the evening says nothing about whether calling at night affects how well the birds coordinate their departures the next morning.

C.recipe: OFF: roost size, a different variable
C.why_wrong: The number of birds at a roost does not show any link between nighttime calling and the coordination of morning departures.

D.recipe: OPP: no difference in coordination
D.why_wrong: If departures were just as synchronized after heavy calling as after quiet nights, nighttime calling would not be interfering with coordination, which weakens the suggestion.

sources.what: Broad, Dibnah, Smith, Thornton 2024, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 379: 20230185: wild jackdaws use vocalizations to coordinate collective movements at winter roosts; roosts in areas with differing degrees of urbanization; with higher background noise, jackdaws took longer to settle in the evening and called more during the night, suggesting sleep disruption; high overnight calling linked to disruption of vocal consensus decision-making and less cohesive group departures in the morning

items.notes: Medium T1: the key observes the outcome (cohesion of the morning departure) varying with the cause (nighttime calling). D is the opposite; B and C are off-target variables. Key A states, as a finding, the link the study reports ('less cohesive group departures'). The passage gives no study region (not in the abstract).

items.subtype: Data completion: pairwise comparison that illustrates a stated relation (period depends on distance, not size)
items.passage: Saturn’s more than one hundred known moons range from small fragments of ice and rock to Titan, which is wider than the planet Mercury. A moon’s orbital period—the time required to complete one revolution around its planet—depends on the moon’s distance from that planet: the more distant the moon, the longer its orbital period. The moon’s own dimensions, by contrast, have essentially no influence on the duration of its orbit. This relationship helps explain why, among the five moons of Saturn shown in the table, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: Titan, by far the largest of the five moons, also has the longest orbital period, about 16 days.
Rhea and Iapetus, which are similar in size, also have similar orbital periods.
Enceladus, the smallest of the five moons, orbits closer to Saturn than Dione does.
Iapetus, though smaller than Titan, takes about five times as long as Titan to orbit Saturn.

table.title: Five Moons of Saturn
columns: Average distance from Saturn (thousands of km)

items.explanation: The text says that a moon’s orbital period depends on its distance from the planet and that the moon’s own dimensions “have essentially no influence on the duration of its orbit.” The table shows that Iapetus (radius 734 km) is much smaller than Titan (2,575 km) but nearly three times as far from Saturn, and its orbital period (79.3 days) is about five times Titan’s (15.9 days). Choice D shows a smaller but more distant moon taking longer to orbit, as the relationship predicts.

A.recipe: INACC: wrong extreme
A.why_wrong: Titan is the largest moon, but Iapetus, not Titan, has the longest orbital period (79.3 days).

B.recipe: INACC: sameness offered where the data differ
B.why_wrong: Rhea and Iapetus are similar in size (764 and 734 km), but their orbital periods are very different: 4.5 days and 79.3 days.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports an ability claim in one step (animals treat two facial expressions differently)
items.passage: Dogs and horses, which were domesticated to work closely with people, can respond to human facial expressions, but little is known about animals raised mainly for milk and meat. items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ conclusion?
options: Goats moved around the enclosure more slowly during their first trial than during later trials, once the setting had become familiar.
Goats that had often been handled by people approached the wall with the photographs sooner than goats that had rarely been handled.
Goats more often went first to the photograph of the smiling face than to the photograph of the angry face.
Goats spent about as much time near the photograph of the angry face as near the photograph of the smiling face.
items.explanation: The researchers concluded that goats “can distinguish between happy and angry human faces.” If goats more often went first to the smiling face than to the angry face, they treated the two expressions differently, so they must have been able to tell them apart. Choice C therefore supports the conclusion.

A.recipe: OFF: a change across trials, not a response to the expressions
A.why_wrong: How quickly goats moved around the enclosure in early and later trials says nothing about whether they could tell a smiling face from an angry one.

B.recipe: OFF: a different variable (experience with people)
B.why_wrong: This links how soon goats approached the photographs to how often they had been handled, not to which facial expression the photographs showed.

D.recipe: OPP: no difference between the faces
D.why_wrong: If goats treated the two faces the same way, there would be no sign that they could tell the expressions apart, so this would weaken the conclusion.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a single-trait claim (works with machinelike speed and precision)
items.passage: “The Romance of a Busy Broker” is a short story in O. Henry’s 1906 collection The Four Million. In the story, Harvey Maxwell, a New York stockbroker, has an especially busy day at his office. The narrator describes Maxwell as working with the speed and precision of a machine: ______

“[Maxwell] was working like some high-geared, delicate, strong machine—strung to full tension, going at full speed, accurate, never hesitating, with the proper word and decision and act ready and prompt as clockwork.”
“On the Exchange there were hurricanes and landslides and snowstorms and glaciers and volcanoes, and those elemental disturbances were reproduced in miniature in the broker’s offices.”
“Maxwell stood by his desk with his hands full of telegrams and memoranda, with a fountain pen over his right ear and his hair hanging in disorderly strings over his forehead.”

Choice B compares Maxwell to a “high-geared, delicate, strong machine” that is “going at full speed” and is “accurate, never hesitating,” acting “prompt as clockwork.” That description shows both his speed and his precision.

A.why_wrong: A clerk calls Maxwell “absent-minded and forgetful,” which is the opposite of the precise, machinelike work the claim describes.

C.recipe: OFF: the busy setting, not Maxwell
C.why_wrong: This describes the turmoil on the stock exchange and in the office, not the way Maxwell himself works.

D.recipe: OFF: Maxwell’s untidy appearance

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a claim (training of young potters; the key supplies the missing premise that teaching leaves two makers’ prints on one vessel)
items.passage: Because the ridges of fingerprints broaden as a person matures, the average ridge width in a print can be used to estimate the approximate age of the individual who left it. Applying this technique to 112 fingerprints impressed into the clay of vessels manufactured between about 2850 and 2500 BCE in an urban neighborhood at Tell eṣ-Ṣâfi/Gath, in present-day Israel, archaeologist Kent D. Fowler and colleagues determined that most of the prints had been left by adults or by adolescents. The researchers propose that in this community, young potters acquired their craft by working under the supervision of experienced practitioners.
items.stem: Which finding from Fowler and colleagues’ study, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ proposal about young potters?
options: Most vessels bearing an adolescent’s prints also bear an adult’s prints, on surfaces that were shaped and smoothed while the vessel was being built.
Prints left by adolescents are about as common on vessels from the earliest layers of the neighborhood as on vessels from its most recent layers.
Vessels bearing only adolescents’ prints are about as numerous, and as evenly shaped and as carefully smoothed, as vessels that bear only adults’ prints.
Most of the prints on the vessels, whether they were left by adults or by adolescents, appear to have been made by males rather than by females.
items.explanation: The researchers propose that “young potters acquired their craft by working under the supervision of experienced practitioners.” Learning under supervision means that a novice and an experienced potter handled the same pieces of work. If vessels with an adolescent’s prints usually also carry an adult’s prints on surfaces formed during building, the two worked on those vessels together, which is what training of this kind would leave behind. Choice A therefore supports the proposal.

B.recipe: TRAP: wrong time window, consistent with both
B.why_wrong: It shows only that adolescents made pottery throughout the neighborhood’s history; adolescents working on their own would leave the same pattern, so it says nothing about whether they were guided by experienced potters.

C.recipe: OPP: competent independent work by adolescents, no sign of supervision
C.why_wrong: Many well-made vessels handled by adolescents alone would suggest that adolescents could work competently on their own; this says nothing about whether they learned the craft under the supervision of experienced potters, and it points away from the proposal.

D.recipe: OFF: same prints, different variable (sex)
D.why_wrong: Whether the potters were mostly male concerns who made pottery, not whether young potters were taught by experienced ones.

sources.what: Fowler, Ross, Walker, Barritt-Cleary, Greenfield, Maeir, Biehl 2020, PLoS ONE 15(4): e0231046: mean ridge breadth (age) and ridge density (sex) of 112 fingerprints on Early Bronze Age III (c. 2850–2500 BCE) pottery from the urban neighbourhood at Tell eṣ-Ṣâfi/Gath, Israel; most prints by adult and young males, the rest by adult and young females; multiple prints of different age and sex on the same vessels suggest they were impressed during the training of young potters

items.notes: Band-7 moves: the claim is stated as guidance of novices; the key supplies the unstated premise that teaching leaves two makers’ prints on surfaces formed during building, the very pattern the authors read as training. B TRAP (time window, fits independent work too), C OPP (many well-finished vessels by adolescents alone; reviewer rewrote it so it no longer negates the key's co-occurrence), D OFF (sex of potters, true in the study but beside the point). Three steps: guidance implies shared work, shared work leaves co-occurring prints, the key reports that co-occurrence. The paper's age classes are adult/adolescent and child; children's prints (only on handles) are left out to avoid a second training reading.
band7_moves: key supplies the missing premise (guidance leaves two makers’ prints on one vessel)
TRAP distractor consistent with both readings (time window)
stem names the study and the claimant

fixes: rewrote option C so it no longer negates the key's co-occurrence (it read as A's mirror image, the band-7 pilot tell); C now reports many well-finished vessels by adolescents alone
shortened key A so it is not the longest option

band7.why: After the reviewer's fix to C: 100-word passage, 19-word stem naming the study, and the key supplies a premise the passage leaves out (supervised work leaves two makers' prints on surfaces formed during building). B is a TRAP (time window, fits independent work too), C an OPP that no longer mirrors the key, D the one OFF option. Passes checks 1, 2, 5 and 6.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a claim (fossil sea cow as a seagrass grazer; the feeding link is given in the passage)
items.passage: Because seagrass seldom fossilizes, paleontologists often reconstruct ancient seagrass meadows from the remains of the animals that consumed them. Dugongs, for example, subsist almost entirely on seagrass, which they uproot from the seabed with their downturned snouts. In Qatar, Nicholas D. Pyenson and colleagues documented more than 170 sites, concentrated in an area smaller than a square kilometer and all within a single layer of rock at least 21 million years old, that contain fossil bones of an extinct sea cow, Salwasiren qatarensis. The researchers suggest that Salwasiren, like the dugongs inhabiting the region today, was a seagrass grazer.
items.stem: Which finding about Salwasiren, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ suggestion?
options: Salwasiren was only distantly related to the dugongs that live in the region today.
Salwasiren’s teeth show the kind of wear seen in living animals that crush the shells of clams and snails.
Several Salwasiren bones bear bite marks left by large sharks, which also prey on the dugongs that live in the region today.
The front of Salwasiren’s skull angles steeply downward, so its mouth would have faced the seafloor, as a dugong’s does.
items.explanation: The researchers suggest that Salwasiren “was a seagrass grazer,” and the passage explains that dugongs “uproot” seagrass “from the seabed with their downturned snouts.” A skull whose front angles steeply downward, leaving the mouth facing the seafloor as a dugong’s does, shows that Salwasiren was built to feed on the seabed in the way dugongs do. Choice D therefore supports the suggestion that it grazed on seagrass.

A.recipe: TRAP: true of the species, but ancestry cannot decide diet
A.why_wrong: How closely Salwasiren was related to today’s dugongs says nothing about what it ate; closely and distantly related animals can share a diet or differ in one.

B.recipe: OPP: a rival diet
B.why_wrong: Tooth wear like that of shell-crushing animals would suggest that Salwasiren fed on clams and snails, which would weaken, not support, the suggestion that it grazed on seagrass.

C.recipe: TRAP: shares a predator with dugongs, not a diet
C.why_wrong: Being hunted by the same kind of predator as today’s dugongs shows nothing about what Salwasiren itself ate.

sources.what: Pyenson, Sakal, LeBlanc, Blundell, Klim, Marshall, Velez-Juarbe, Wolfe, Al-Naimi 2025, PeerJ 13: e20030 (doi 10.7717/peerj.20030), High abundance of Early Miocene sea cows from Qatar shows repeated evolution of seagrass ecosystem engineers in Eastern Tethys: seagrasses rarely fossilize and their consumers serve as proxies; over 172 sites in less than 1 km2 from one stratigraphic level (Al Maszhabiya bonebed, Aquitanian, 23.03 to 21.6 Ma); new dugongine Salwasiren qatarensis, distantly related to extant dugongs, which occupy seagrass habitats of the Gulf today; premaxilla shows the deflection of the distal rostrum seen in most dugongids; seagrass consumers have evolved repeatedly in the region at least since the Early Miocene

items.notes: Reviewer replacement: the earlier subject (melanosomes or microbes in a fossil feather) shares its premise with official Inferences item eca09a92 (melanosomes in a fossil feather reveal an extinct bird's color). Band 6: the feeding link sits in an earlier sentence (dugongs uproot seagrass from the seabed with downturned snouts); the key paraphrases it (skull angled down, mouth facing the seafloor) and needs one bridge. The key fits the real anatomy (rostral deflection like most dugongids). A is true in the study but cannot decide diet; C ties Salwasiren to dugongs through predators, not food; B is the rival diet. No option uses abundance or a shallow-water setting, since the paper itself reads those as signs of seagrass habitat.
