items.subtype: Finding that discriminates two explanations (conformity versus public information)
items.passage: Animals that acquire behaviors by observing others must decide which individuals to imitate: under one strategy, conformity, an animal copies whatever the majority of a group is doing, whereas under another, the use of public information, it evaluates each option according to how successfully others appear to be exploiting it. Edwin van Leeuwen, Thomas Morgan, and Katharina Riebel allowed zebra finches to observe two groups of finches, differing in size, feeding from two unfamiliar feeders, one black and one white, and then recorded which feeder each observer selected. The researchers concluded that zebra finches are not conformists but instead rely on public information.
items.stem: Which finding from the study, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ conclusion?
options: The observers generally chose the feeder used by the larger group, even in trials in which the smaller group pecked at its feeder more often.
When a smaller group pecked at its feeder more often than a larger group pecked at the other feeder, the observers generally chose the smaller group’s feeder.
When the larger group also pecked at its feeder more often than the smaller group did, the observers generally chose the larger group’s feeder.
The observers pecked more often at the black feeder than at the white one, regardless of how many birds they had seen eating from each.
items.explanation: Under conformity an animal “copies whatever the majority of a group is doing,” whereas under the use of public information it “evaluates each option according to how successfully others appear to be exploiting it.” The two strategies point to different feeders only when the smaller group is the busier one. If the observers then chose the smaller group’s feeder, they followed how actively others were feeding rather than how many were feeding, so choice B supports the conclusion.

A.recipe: OPP: the conformity prediction
A.why_wrong: Following the larger group even when the smaller group fed more actively is what conformity predicts, so it would weaken the conclusion.

C.recipe: TRAP: consistent with both strategies
C.why_wrong: When the larger group is also the busier one, conformity and public information both point to its feeder, so this choice cannot show which strategy the birds used.

D.recipe: OFF: a color preference
D.why_wrong: A preference for the black feeder that ignores what the groups did says nothing about whether the birds conform or use public information.

sources.what: van Leeuwen, Morgan, Riebel 2021, Biology Letters 17: 20200767, Foraging zebra finches are public information users rather than conformists: observers watched two demonstrator groups differing in size (ratios 1:2, 2:4, 3:3, 1:5) forage from novel black and white feeders; observers did not copy the majority but were influenced by the demonstrators’ foraging activity (pecks), in an anti-conformist fashion

items.notes: Band 6. The key needs two links: the strategies diverge only when the minority is the busier group, and choosing the minority's feeder then marks public information. Matches the real result (influenced by pecks, not majority).

items.subtype: Finding that discriminates two explanations (eggs versus individual organisms; the key supplies the growth premise)
items.passage: Chitinozoans are microscopic, flask-shaped fossils with tough organic walls that are found in marine rocks formed between about 485 and 359 million years ago. Because individual chitinozoan species appeared and disappeared quickly, geologists use them to date the rock layers in which they occur, yet the question of what kind of organism produced them has never been settled. For decades, most researchers have treated chitinozoans as the eggs of some unidentified marine animal. After examining many well-preserved specimens of a newly described species, Hercochitina violana, Yan Liang and colleagues argued instead that chitinozoans may not have been eggs at all but rather individual microorganisms.
items.stem: Which finding about Hercochitina violana, if true, would most directly support Liang and colleagues’ argument?
options: Specimens of H. violana are often found joined end to end in chains, an arrangement that resembles the strings of eggs laid by some living marine worms.
Specimens of H. violana vary in size by about as much as the specimens of most other chitinozoan species do.
Specimens of H. violana form an unbroken series running from small, simple forms to large forms with elaborate surface ornamentation.
H. violana occurs only in rocks from a brief interval of geologic time, which makes it especially useful for dating the layers in which it is found.
items.explanation: Liang and colleagues argue that chitinozoans “may not have been eggs at all but rather individual microorganisms.” An egg is formed at more or less its final size and structure, whereas an organism grows and develops. An unbroken series running from small, simple specimens to large, elaborately ornamented ones looks like the growth stages of a single kind of organism, which fits the researchers’ view and not the egg interpretation. Choice C therefore supports their argument.

A.recipe: OPP: fits the egg view
A.why_wrong: Chains resembling the egg strings of living marine worms would make chitinozoans look more like eggs, supporting the interpretation the researchers reject.

B.recipe: TRAP: comparison that cannot decide
B.why_wrong: Comparing H. violana only with other chitinozoans says nothing about how chitinozoans differ from eggs, so it fits either interpretation.

D.recipe: OFF: an irrelevant property of the same fossils
D.why_wrong: A short time range explains why the species is useful for dating rocks; it does not show whether its specimens were eggs or organisms.

sources.what: Liang, Bernardo, Goldman, Nõlvak, Tang, Wang, Hints 2019, Proceedings of the Royal Society B 286: 20191270: chitinozoans, organic-walled microfossils of Ordovician to Devonian age (ca 485–359 Ma) used in biostratigraphy, of unknown affinity and most commonly interpreted as eggs of marine metazoans; the size variation within chitinozoan species is larger than in fossil and modern eggs; distinct and continuous morphological variation in the new species Hercochitina violana is more plausibly an ontogenetic series of individual microorganisms than eggs

items.notes: Band-7 moves: the passage gives only the two views; the key supplies the growth (ontogeny) premise that eggs do not develop progressively, matching the authors' reading of H. violana. A OPP (chains fit egg strings; chitinozoan chains are real and long cited for the egg view), B TRAP (within-chitinozoan comparison), D OFF (biostratigraphic use).
band7_moves: key supplies the missing premise (a growth series implies a developing organism)
TRAP distractor with a comparison that cannot decide
OPP distractor fitting the rival view
stem names the claimant and the rival

band7.why: The key adds the growth premise the passage omits (an organism grows from small, simple to large, ornate forms; an egg does not). Discrimination: the egg view predicts no growth series, the organism view predicts one; B (size variation compared only with other chitinozoans) is a TRAP that fits both, A fits the egg view, D is an irrelevant property. 104-word passage, 15-word stem naming the claimants. Passes checks 1, 2, 5, 6 and 7.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates an indirect claim (translated drama; parts of one story as options)
items.passage: The Lower Depths is a 1902 play by Maxim Gorky, translated by Jenny Covan in 1922. In the play, Luka, an elderly wanderer lodging among the destitute, intimates that a consoling belief can matter more to a suffering person than the truth does: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from a translation of The Lower Depths most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “He said: ‘Somewhere on this earth there must be a righteous land—and wonderful people live there—good people! They respect each other, help each other, and everything is peaceful and good!’”
“The learned man was offended. ‘My plans,’ he said, ‘are correct. But there exists no land of righteousness anywhere.’”
“Some one has to be kind, girl—some one must pity people! Christ pitied everybody—and he said to us: ‘Go and do likewise!’”
“He’d lived and lived and suffered and suffered, and had believed all the time in the existence of this land—and now, according to the plans, it didn’t exist at all. He felt robbed!”
items.explanation: The claim is that Luka intimates that “a consoling belief can matter more to a suffering person than the truth does.” In choice D, Luka describes a man who had “suffered and suffered” while believing in a land that, once the truth was shown on the maps, “didn’t exist at all,” leaving him feeling “robbed.” The man lost something of value when the truth replaced his belief, which is exactly what the claim describes.

A.recipe: HALF: the belief without the truth that undoes it
A.why_wrong: It presents the man’s hopeful belief in a righteous land but says nothing about the truth or about what the belief was worth to him compared with it.

B.recipe: HALF: the truth without its cost
B.why_wrong: It states the truth, that no such land exists, but not the belief it destroys or the harm done to a suffering man.

C.recipe: OFF: same speaker, nearby value (pity)
C.why_wrong: Luka urges kindness and pity toward others, but he does not weigh a consoling belief against the truth.

sources.what: Maxim Gorky, The Lower Depths: A Drama in Four Acts, English translation by Jenny Covan (New York: Brentano’s, 1922, Moscow Art Theatre Series of Russian Plays); Act III, Luka’s story of the man who believed in a land of righteousness and the learned man’s maps; Luka’s lines on pity to Natasha; all four quotations checked as exact substrings of the Gutenberg text (double hyphens as closed em dashes, inner double quotes as single quotes)

items.notes: Play first performed 1902 (Moscow Art Theatre). Three options come from the same story, so the key must be matched to both parts of the claim (belief and truth weighed); C is Luka in a nearby mood (pity). Lines where Luka tells Nastya that a believed love affair was real were left out (they would also illustrate the claim).

items.subtype: Data description (interaction: each color of lizard compared across the two grounds)
items.passage: Camouflage protects an animal only when its coloration matches the surrounding terrain, and in northwestern China the toad-headed lizard Phrynocephalus versicolor has evolved dark coloration where the ground is dark while retaining lighter coloration in neighboring areas where the ground is pale. Lixia Wan and colleagues tested the hypothesis that a lizard runs faster on ground it does not match, where it must depend on speed rather than concealment, by timing dark and light lizards in racing tunnels positioned on both kinds of ground. Examining the results, a student concludes that the hypothesis was supported for light lizards but not for dark lizards.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the student’s conclusion?
options: On dark ground, light lizards ran faster than dark lizards, 0.821 compared with 0.626 meters per second, but on pale ground they ran slower than dark lizards, 0.558 compared with 0.609.
Light lizards ran much faster on dark ground than on pale ground, 0.821 compared with 0.558 meters per second, whereas dark lizards ran at nearly equal speeds on the two, 0.626 and 0.609.
Dark lizards ran faster on pale ground, which they do not match, than on dark ground, while light lizards ran at almost the same speed whichever kind of ground they were on.
Light lizards ran faster on dark ground, which they do not match, than on pale ground, which they do match, 0.821 compared with 0.558 meters per second.

table.title: Average Running Speed of Toad-Headed Lizards on Two Kinds of Ground (meters per second)

items.explanation: The student concludes that “the hypothesis was supported for light lizards but not for dark lizards.” Light lizards match pale ground, and they ran much faster on dark ground (0.821 meters per second) than on pale ground (0.558), as the hypothesis predicts. Dark lizards match dark ground, yet they ran at nearly equal speeds on dark ground (0.626) and on pale ground (0.609), so they did not run faster on the ground they do not match. Choice B reports both halves.

A.recipe: IRREL: accurate comparison on the wrong axis (colors within one ground)
A.why_wrong: The values are read correctly, but they compare light and dark lizards on the same ground; the hypothesis concerns how each lizard’s speed changes between ground it matches and ground it does not.

C.recipe: WDIR/INACC: the pattern assigned to the wrong lizards
C.why_wrong: The table shows the reverse: dark lizards ran at almost the same speed on both grounds (0.626 and 0.609), and light lizards were the ones whose speed differed greatly.

D.recipe: HALF: accurate for light lizards only
D.why_wrong: The reading is accurate, but it covers only light lizards; the student’s conclusion also says the hypothesis did not hold for dark lizards, which this choice does not address.

sources.what: Wan, Liu, Wang, Yang, Li, Sun, Niu, Zhao, Jin 2021, Ecology and Evolution 11: 17409–17416 (doi 10.1002/ece3.8374): Phrynocephalus versicolor evolved darker dorsal color in melanistic habitats and kept a lighter color in adjacent non-melanistic habitats; hypothesis that lizards run more slowly on well-matching backgrounds; running speed measured in field racing tunnels placed on melanistic and non-melanistic substrates; average speed (m/s) light lizards 0.821 on melanistic, 0.558 on non-melanistic; dark lizards 0.626 on melanistic, 0.609 on non-melanistic

items.notes: The conclusion is given to a student (the paper says only that light lizards are potentially faster than dark ones in melanistic habitats). 'Dark ground' and 'pale ground' stand for the paper's melanistic and non-melanistic substrates. Checked: both lizards ran faster on dark ground, so no option says that (it would also support the conclusion).

items.subtype: Quotation from an art historian supports a student’s argument (technique tied to purpose)
items.passage: The Indonesian painter Affandi (circa 1907–1990), who was largely self-taught, became known in the 1950s for an unconventional technique. Rather than applying oil paint with a brush, he squeezed it directly from the tube onto the canvas and then manipulated it with his fingers and palms. A student argues that this technique was considerably more than a recognizable signature, contending that it was Affandi’s means of transferring the emotions a subject aroused in him onto the canvas as immediately as possible.
items.stem: Which quotation from an art historian would best support the student’s argument?
options: “Working straight from the tube with his bare hands, Affandi could set down what a beggar or a crowded market made him feel before the feeling cooled; the thick, twisting ridges of paint carry an agitation that a brush would have smoothed away.”

“The tube method began as a practical shortcut—Affandi, impatient, had been unable to find a pencil—and it remained chiefly that: an efficient way to cover a canvas, revealing more about his working habits than about what he hoped his paintings would express.”

“His canvases are built from coils and ribbons of pigment applied so heavily that, viewed from the side, the surface rises in ridges several millimeters high, and in places the colors, pressed together by his palm, mix directly on the canvas.”

“Affandi declined to paint the pleasant landscapes that collectors requested, choosing instead an old woman, a beggar, a dark mountain—subjects he considered expressive rather than beautiful—and returning to them repeatedly throughout his career.”
items.explanation: The student contends that the technique “was Affandi’s means of transferring the emotions a subject aroused in him onto the canvas as immediately as possible.” Choice A ties the technique to exactly that aim: working from the tube with his hands let Affandi record what a subject made him feel before the feeling faded, and the ridges of paint preserve an agitation a brush would have erased.

B.recipe: OPP: sides with the view the student rejects
B.why_wrong: It presents the procedure as a mere convenience that says little about what the paintings express, which contradicts the student’s argument.

C.recipe: HALF: the technique described, without its purpose
C.why_wrong: It describes how thickly the paint was applied and how colors mixed, but it never links the technique to the feelings Affandi wanted to convey.

D.recipe: TRAP: expressiveness through subject matter, not technique
D.why_wrong: It shows that Affandi chose expressive subjects, but the student’s argument concerns his technique of applying paint, which this quotation does not mention.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Affandi (c. 1907–1990), Indonesian painter, self-taught from 1934, considered Indonesia’s foremost Expressionist; from the 1950s painted by squeezing paint directly from the tube (Carrying the First Grandchild, 1953), found the painted object appeared more alive and felt more freedom to express his feelings using his hands instead of a brush; adopted the method after losing patience looking for a missing pencil; painted suffering (an old woman, a beggar, a black mountain), subjects expressive rather than beautiful

items.notes: Quotations are invented and attributed to an unnamed art historian, as CB does; their factual content follows the source (the pencil story, the subjects he named). Band 6: the key must be matched to the argument's link between procedure and emotion; D (subject matter) and C (technique alone) each match half.

items.subtype: Data completion (the heaviest treatment compared with the untreated control)
items.passage: Spreading organic mulch, such as wood chips, over bare soil can reduce runoff during heavy rainfall and allow more water to infiltrate the ground, but because mulch also absorbs water, a thick layer may retain rain that would otherwise reach the soil. At Jiufeng National Forest Park in Beijing, Bing Wang and colleagues covered trays of sloping soil with different quantities of mulch, subjected them to simulated rainstorms of two intensities, and measured how much water the soil stored. Comparing the mulched soil with bare soil, the team found that heavier applications of mulch did not continue to improve water storage: ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
options: soil covered with 0.25 kilogram of mulch per square meter stored less water than bare soil did under both rainfall intensities.
at the higher rainfall intensity, soil under 1.00 kilogram of mulch per square meter stored nearly twice as much water as bare soil.
with 1.00 kilogram of mulch per square meter, the soil stored about as much water as bare soil did at either rainfall intensity.
the lightest mulch layer, 0.25 kilogram per square meter, raised the amount of water stored in the soil above that of bare soil at both intensities.

figure.title: Water Stored in Soil under Different Amounts of Mulch during Simulated Heavy Rain
figure.description: Grouped bars at five mulch amounts (0, which is bare soil; 0.25; 0.50; 0.75; 1.00 kilograms per square meter), two bars each: rainfall of 60 millimeters per hour and rainfall of 90 millimeters per hour. Y-axis 0 to 25 in steps of 5. 60 mm/h: about 12.6, 19.8, 16.4, 13.8, 12.4. 90 mm/h: about 12.5, 22.7, 20.3, 16.6, 13.1. At both intensities storage is highest at 0.25 and falls with each heavier layer, back to about the bare-soil level at 1.00.

items.explanation: The team found that “heavier applications of mulch did not continue to improve water storage.” The graph shows that with 1.00 kilogram of mulch per square meter, the heaviest layer tested, the soil stored about 12.4 millimeters of water at 60 millimeters of rain per hour and about 13.1 millimeters at 90, close to the 12.6 and 12.5 millimeters stored by bare soil. Since the heaviest layer gave almost no gain over bare soil, choice C completes the statement.

A.recipe: WDIR: the lightest layer reported below bare soil
A.why_wrong: Soil under 0.25 kilogram of mulch stored the most water of all, about 19.8 and 22.7 millimeters, well above bare soil’s 12.6 and 12.5.

B.recipe: INACC: invented gain
B.why_wrong: At 90 millimeters per hour, soil under 1.00 kilogram of mulch stored about 13.1 millimeters, barely more than the 12.5 stored by bare soil, not nearly twice as much.

D.recipe: IRREL: true, but about the light layer only
D.why_wrong: The graph does show that the lightest layer raised storage above bare soil, but that says nothing about whether heavier layers kept improving storage, which is what the statement is about.

sources.what: Wang, Niu, Berndtsson, Zhang, Chen, Li, Zhu 2021, Scientific Reports 11: 6259 (doi 10.1038/s41598-021-85343-x): rainfall simulation experiments with organic mulch (ground wood residue, wood chips and straw) in Jiufeng National Forestry Park, Beijing; soil water storage (mm), 15° slope, mulch 0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00 kg/m2: 60 mm/h 12.6, 19.8, 16.4, 13.8, 12.4; 90 mm/h 12.5, 22.7, 20.3, 16.6, 13.1; higher application rates gave less soil water

items.notes: Graph uses the paper's 15-degree slope values (Table 1). Checked in Python: only C is true and bears on the claim; D is true but concerns the light layer only. No option compares 0.50 with 0.25 (that comparison would also support the statement).

items.subtype: Data completion (two comparisons in different years: an early lead later lost)
items.passage: Over the 2010s, solar power grew from a negligible source of electricity into a substantial one in several countries, although the trajectories differed considerably from one country to another. In some countries, an early burst of construction was followed by years of little further expansion, while countries whose solar industries developed more gradually continued adding capacity and eventually matched or surpassed those early leaders. Examining figures for 2013 through 2021 compiled by Ember, an independent energy research organization, a student finds that Honduras exemplifies the first of these patterns: according to the graph, the share of Honduras’s electricity generated from solar power ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
options: was greater than Chile’s in both 2015 and 2017.
was lower than Vietnam’s in 2017 but higher than Vietnam’s in 2021.
rose steadily throughout the period and in 2021 was higher than the share in any other country shown.
was more than twice Jordan’s in 2017 but was lower than Jordan’s in 2021.

figure.title: Share of Electricity Generated from Solar Power in Four Countries, 2013–2021
figure.y_axis: Percent of electricity generated from solar power
figure.description: Four lines at 2013, 2015, 2017, 2019 and 2021; y-axis 0 to 16 in steps of 2. Honduras: about 0, 4.9, 9.9, 10.5, 10.3 (a sharp rise to 2017, then nearly flat). Jordan: about 0, 0.3, 4.4, 10.0, 15.4 (rises steadily and is highest in 2021). Chile: about 0, 1.7, 4.9, 7.5, 12.0. Vietnam: about 0, 0, 0, 2.0, 10.3 (near zero until 2017, then a steep rise). In 2017 Honduras is highest; by 2021 Jordan and Chile are above Honduras and Vietnam is level with it.

items.explanation: The student says Honduras exemplifies the pattern in which “an early burst of construction was followed by years of little further expansion” while slower countries “eventually matched or surpassed those early leaders.” The graph shows Honduras at about 9.9% in 2017, more than twice Jordan’s 4.4%, but at about 10.3% in 2021, below Jordan’s 15.4%. Choice D shows Honduras leading early and then being overtaken.

A.recipe: PART: accurate early comparison only
A.why_wrong: Honduras’s share was indeed above Chile’s in 2015 and 2017, but this shows only the early lead, not that a more gradual country later matched or overtook Honduras.

B.recipe: WDIR: comparison reversed
B.why_wrong: In 2017 Honduras’s share (about 9.9%) was far higher than Vietnam’s (near 0%), and in 2021 the two were nearly equal, so neither half of the statement is accurate.

C.recipe: INACC: contradicts the pattern
C.why_wrong: Honduras’s share leveled off after 2017, and in 2021 it was below Jordan’s and Chile’s, so it neither rose steadily nor ended highest.

sources.what: Our World in Data, Share of electricity production from solar (Ember), percent: Honduras 2013 0.0, 2015 4.88, 2017 9.91, 2019 10.51, 2021 10.25; Jordan 0.0, 0.26, 4.38, 10.03, 15.40; Chile 0.01, 1.66, 4.87, 7.50, 11.99; Vietnam 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 2.03, 10.31

items.notes: Every option checked in Python against the values. Vietnam also catches up with Honduras by 2021 (10.31 against 10.25), so no option states that true Vietnam comparison; B reverses it and is false in both halves. Ember describes itself as an independent energy think tank.

fixes: passage said the burst came 'early in the decade', but Honduras's rise runs 2013 to 2017 on the graph; now 'an early burst of construction' (explanation quote updated)
first sentence lengthened slightly to stay near the models' median length

items.subtype: Data completion (filter by a criterion stated in the passage, then the maximum)
items.passage: Agricultural surveys frequently estimate a field’s yield by harvesting only a small portion of it and extrapolating from the result, because harvesting an entire field is slow and costly. Using complete harvests of 230 smallholder maize fields in Ethiopia as the standard, Tesfaye Shiferaw Sida and colleagues determined how often several such shortcut methods produced an estimate within 10% of a field’s true yield. A student designing a survey in which workers can harvest no more than 20 square meters of each field observes that, among the methods respecting that restriction, the one most likely to produce an estimate within 10% of the true yield was ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: the random quadrat, which harvests 16 square meters of each field and came within 10% of the true yield in about 25% of cases.
the random octant, which came within 10% of the true yield in about 30% of cases, more often than any other method in the table.
the three diagonal quadrats, which together harvest 48 square meters of each field and came within 10% of the true yield in about 28% of cases.
the horizontal transect, which harvests only 4 square meters of each field and came within 10% of the true yield in about 20% of cases.

table.title: Accuracy of Five Methods for Estimating Maize Yield on Smallholder Fields in Ethiopia
columns: Chance of an estimate within 10% of true yield (%)
table.note: *Average; the octant is one-eighth of the field, so its area ranged from 47 to 690 square meters.

items.explanation: The student’s survey allows workers to harvest “no more than 20 square meters of each field.” Only the MW path (10 square meters), the horizontal transect (4), and the random quadrat (16) respect that restriction. Of these three, the random quadrat had the highest chance of an estimate within 10% of the true yield, 25.2%, compared with 19.5% and 17.8%. Choice A therefore completes the statement.

B.recipe: TRAP: the overall maximum, outside the passage's limit
B.why_wrong: The random octant was the most accurate method overall, but it harvests about 177 square meters, far more than the 20-square-meter limit, so it is not among the methods the student is considering.

C.recipe: TRAP: second-highest overall, outside the limit
C.why_wrong: The three diagonal quadrats harvest 48 square meters in total, which exceeds the student’s limit.

D.recipe: WGRP: within the limit but not the most accurate
D.why_wrong: The horizontal transect stays within the limit, but its chance of an estimate within 10%, about 20%, is lower than the random quadrat’s 25.2%.

sources.what: Sida, Chamberlin, Ayalew, Kosmowski, Craufurd 2021, Field Crops Research 267: 108147 (doi 10.1016/j.fcr.2021.108147, PMC8146729): full plot harvests of 230 smallholder maize fields in Ethiopia; sampling area per method (m2): MW path 10, horizontal transect 4, random quadrat 16, three diagonal quadrats 48, random octant 177 (47–690); probability of an estimate within 10% of the true yield: 0.178, 0.195, 0.252, 0.284, 0.298

items.notes: Band-7 moves (Q1_P2, model 3.44): a filter set by a criterion stated only in the passage (the 20-square-meter limit), then a maximum; the two most accurate methods overall are traps outside the limit (TRAP), and one in-limit method is less accurate. Farmer prediction and the full harvest are left out of the table. Operations: read the limit, filter three rows by area, compare three values.
band7_moves: filter set by a passage criterion before the extreme
traps are the overall maxima outside the filter
compound options naming method, area and value

fixes: table note now gives the octant's real range (47 to 690 square meters, Sida et al. Table 1) so no small field's octant can be read as under the 20-square-meter limit
passage and options lengthened a little to band-7 lengths (passage 107 words, options 24 to 26 words)

B and C are accurate overall maxima outside the filter and D is accurate but not the maximum, so all three distractors are accurate readings. items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a two-part claim (attraction and unease)
items.passage: The Ladies’ Paradise is an 1883 novel by Émile Zola. Newly arrived in Paris from a provincial town, Denise first encounters the enormous department store that gives the novel its title. Zola portrays her as simultaneously attracted to the store and apprehensive about it: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Ladies’ Paradise most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “At this hour, The Ladies’ Paradise, with its furnace-like brilliancy, completed its conquest of her. In the great metropolis, black and silent beneath the rain—in this Paris, to which she was a stranger, it shone out like a lighthouse, and seemed to be of itself the life and light of the city.”
“At the same time her uncle’s shop made her feel ill at ease; she felt unreasonable disdain, instinctive repugnance for this cold, icy place, the home of old-fashioned trading.”

“She was bewildered and attracted by this shop, to her so vast, which she saw more people enter in an hour than she had seen enter Cornaille’s in six months; and with her desire to enter it was mingled a vague sense of danger which rendered her seduction complete.”
“There was the continual roaring of a machine at work, an engulfing of customers close-pressed against the counters, bewildered amidst the piles of goods, and finally hurled towards the pay-desks.”
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Denise is “attracted to the store” and “apprehensive about it.” In choice C, she is “attracted by this shop” and feels a “desire to enter it,” and with that desire “was mingled a vague sense of danger,” so the quotation shows both her attraction and her apprehension.

A.recipe: HALF: attraction only
A.why_wrong: The store “completed its conquest of her” and shines “like a lighthouse,” which shows only her attraction, not any apprehension.

B.recipe: LURE: unease, but about the wrong shop
B.why_wrong: Denise feels ill at ease here, but about her uncle’s old-fashioned shop, not the department store.

D.recipe: LURE: shares the word “bewildered,” describes the customers

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a claim (group comparison: listening expertise)
items.passage: Orchestral sample libraries are collections of recordings of single notes played on real instruments, which composers can put together on a computer to imitate a full orchestra. In an online experiment, music psychologist Reinhard Kopiez and colleagues asked more than 600 listeners with different amounts of musical and audio training to judge whether excerpts of a classical work had been played by a live orchestra or made with such a library. The researchers hypothesized that listeners’ skill at judging sound would affect how well they could tell the two kinds of recording apart.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ hypothesis?
options: Most listeners described the live orchestra recordings as more pleasant to hear than the recordings that had been produced with the sample library.
Listeners who work professionally with recorded sound identified the source of the excerpts correctly more often than other listeners did.
Listeners identified the source of slow, quiet excerpts correctly more often than they identified the source of fast, loud excerpts.
On average, the listeners in the experiment identified the source of the excerpts correctly about 72 percent of the time.
items.explanation: The researchers hypothesized that “listeners’ skill at judging sound would affect how well they could tell the two kinds of recording apart.” If listeners whose work involves judging recorded sound identified the source correctly more often than other listeners, accuracy would differ with skill, as the hypothesis predicts. Choice B therefore supports it.

A.recipe: OFF: preference, not accuracy
A.why_wrong: Which recordings listeners enjoyed more says nothing about how accurately listeners of different expertise could identify them.

C.recipe: OFF: a property of the music, not of the listeners
C.why_wrong: A difference between kinds of excerpts concerns the music, not whether listeners’ expertise affected their accuracy.

D.recipe: PART: overall accuracy with no comparison between groups
D.why_wrong: An average for all listeners does not show whether more expert listeners did better than less expert ones.

The Discernibility of Sample Library and Live Orchestra Sounds: online experiment with 602 listeners judging whether a classical orchestral work was a live recording or produced with an orchestral sample library; overall 72.5% correct; sound experts tended to identify the source correctly, listeners with lower expertise 68.6% (80.0% for high sound-discrimination expertise); the study tested the influence of listening expertise

items.notes: Medium: the key needs the comparison group (expert against other listeners). D uses the study's real overall figure (72.5%, about 72 percent) as an accurate but comparison-free distractor. Kopiez is a professor of music psychology at the Hanover University of Music, Drama and Media.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a claim (a behavior is maladaptive; the key shows the better alternative)
items.passage: Female common glow-worms, beetles found across much of Europe, glow at night to attract flying males, which find the females by their light. Because artificial light can make that glow harder for males to see, Christina Elgert and colleagues studied how females respond to it. Females exposed to artificial light did not move away but instead delayed glowing or did not glow at all. The researchers argue that this response is maladaptive: by staying where they are, females give up mating opportunities that moving could have provided.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ argument?
options: Females that delayed glowing in artificial light went on to glow for longer, once they began, than females in darkness did.
Glowing dummy females set beneath a simulated streetlight attracted as many males as dummies set a few meters away.
Glow-worm larvae, which also give off light, were about as common near streetlights as in nearby areas without artificial light.
Glowing dummy females placed a few meters from a simulated streetlight attracted more males than dummies placed directly beneath it.
items.explanation: The researchers argue that “by staying where they are, females give up mating opportunities that moving could have provided.” If dummy females a few meters from a streetlight attracted more males than dummies directly beneath it, a female that moved a short distance away from the light would attract more mates than one that stayed put. Choice D therefore supports the argument.

A.recipe: OFF: glow duration, no bearing on relocating
A.why_wrong: Glowing longer after a delay says nothing about whether moving away from the light would have brought a female more males.

B.recipe: OPP: no benefit from moving
B.why_wrong: If dummies near and far from the light attracted equal numbers of males, moving away would gain a female nothing, which weakens the argument.

C.recipe: SUBJ: larvae rather than adult females
C.why_wrong: How common the glowing larvae are near lights says nothing about whether adult females would attract more males by moving away from a light.

sources.what: Elgert, Hopkins, Kaitala, Candolin 2020, Proceedings of the Royal Society B 287: 20200806, Reproduction under light pollution: maladaptive response to spatial variation in artificial light in a glow-worm: females of Lampyris noctiluca glow to attract males; exposed to an artificial light gradient they do not move away but delay or refrain from glowing; field study with a simulated streetlight showed that staying still under the light decreases mate attraction, while moving only a short distance from the light markedly improves it

items.notes: The key mirrors the real field result (dummy females at inner versus outer positions around a simulated streetlight). Medium: two links (staying is costly only if relocating helps; the key shows relocating helps).

items.passage: Camera traps can survey wildlife cheaply, but only if the animals they photograph are identified correctly, which is hard when two similar species share a habitat. Fiona McKibben and Jennifer Frey developed a key for telling apart two nearly identical chipmunk species in New Mexico and tested observers on photographs of museum specimens whose species was already known. The researchers concluded that both the key and later training made identifications more accurate and also made observers agree with one another more often.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers’ conclusion?
options: Observers relying on published descriptions were correct 78.2% of the time, whereas observers using the key were correct 93.0% of the time before any training.
Agreement among observers using the key rose from 0.75 before training to 0.95 after it, so after training their identifications were much more consistent than before.
Accuracy and agreement both rose from observers using published descriptions (78.2%, 0.47) to key users before training (93.0%, 0.75) and again after training (98.8%, 0.95).
Observers relying on published descriptions were less accurate than key users after training, 78.2% compared with 93.0%, and agreed with one another far less.

items.explanation: The researchers concluded that “both the key and later training made identifications more accurate and also made observers agree with one another more often.” The table shows accuracy rising from 78.2% with published descriptions to 93.0% with the key and 98.8% after training, while agreement rose from 0.47 to 0.75 to 0.95. items.passage: Physicists Lukas Schneider and Claudius Gros analyzed five decades of weekly album sales charts from the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, and the Netherlands. items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ claim?
options: Albums now tend to reach number one in their first week on a chart, while in earlier decades they usually took over a month to reach the top.
Albums by solo performers spent about as many weeks on the charts as albums by bands and other musical groups did.
The number of different albums reaching number one each year has steadily fallen in all four countries since the 1970s.
Albums that reached number one in the United States usually went on to reach number one in the United Kingdom and in Germany within a few weeks.
items.explanation: The researchers claim that “changes in popular culture now happen faster than they did in the past.” If albums now reach number one right away instead of taking over a month, as they did in earlier decades, the charts are changing more quickly than before. Choice A therefore supports the claim.

B.recipe: OFF: solo performers versus groups

C.recipe: OPP: slower turnover
C.why_wrong: Fewer albums reaching number one each year would mean each one stays on top longer, suggesting slower, not faster, change.

D.recipe: OFF: agreement among countries
D.why_wrong: Whether hits in one country become hits in others concerns how success spreads, not whether it changes faster than it used to.
